rules.title: Auto-deref reference operand to primitive in scalar binops
rules.statement: For binary operators in {+,-,*,/,%,<,<=,>,>=,==,!=,&,|,^,<<,>>}, an operand of type &T or &mut T whose pointee T is an integer, f32, f64, bool, or char is implicitly dereferenced to T before operator resolution; struct pointees are not peeled.
rules.divergence: Models Rust's `impl Add<i32> for &i32` family via auto-deref rather than blanket ref impls.

rules.title: Auto-deref &T for bitwise/shift when T is integer (or bool for bitwise-only)
rules.statement: For bitwise/shift operators {&,|,^,<<,>>}, an operand of type &T is implicitly dereferenced to T when T is an integer type, or when the operator is one of {&,|,^} and T is bool; shift operators never deref a bool pointee.

rules.title: String == str views String as str
rules.statement: For == and !=, when one operand is the struct String and the other is str (Slice<u8>), the String operand is viewed as str via .as_str() so the comparison proceeds through the str equality path.

rules.title: str equality compares contents via str_eq
rules.statement: == / != between two str operands (both Slice<u8> with u8 element) desugar to a call to stdlib `str_eq` (content comparison); != negates the result. With no `str_eq` in scope, falls back to (incorrect) pointer comparison.

rules.title: str ordering via str_cmp compared to 0
rules.statement: Relational operators {<,<=,>,>=} between two str operands desugar to `str_cmp(lhs, rhs) OP 0`, where str_cmp returns lexicographic -1/0/1 (i32).

rules.title: Operator overloading on struct LHS desugars to trait method
rules.statement: When the left operand is a struct, the operator desugars to the corresponding trait method: + Add::add, - Sub::sub, * Mul::mul, / Div::div, % Rem::rem, & BitAnd::bitand, | BitOr::bitor, ^ BitXor::bitxor, << Shl::shl, >> Shr::shr, == Eq::eq, != Eq::ne, < Ord::lt, <= Ord::le, > Ord::gt, >= Ord::ge.

rules.title: Operator-method operands auto-borrowed to match by-ref formals
rules.statement: When the resolved operator-overload method takes an operand by reference (&self / &other), the corresponding value operand is auto-borrowed (addr_of_temp) to match; by-value method formals receive the operand by value unchanged.

rules.title: Relational ops derive from partial_cmp when direct method absent
rules.statement: For a struct LHS with relational op {<,<=,>,>=}, if the direct lt/le/gt/ge method is not implemented but partial_cmp is, the comparison derives as a.partial_cmp(&b) followed by is_lt/is_le/is_gt/is_ge; when partial_cmp returns Option<Ordering> it routes through cmp_opt_is_<op> (None => false), and when it returns Ordering directly it calls Ordering::is_<op>.
rules.divergence: Mirrors Rust's default PartialOrd lt/le/gt/ge bodies.

rules.title: Tuple == / != routes to Eq impl only for non-primitive tuples
rules.statement: == / != between two tuples of equal arity routes to the tuple's Eq eq/ne impl (keyed concrete `$tuple$N$...`, then arity `$tuple$N`, then variadic `$tuple$variadic`) ONLY when at least one field is non-primitive; an all-primitive tuple falls through to per-field value comparison and never requires the Eq trait. Operands are auto-borrowed to &Tuple.
rules.divergence: Primitive-tuple fast path avoids requiring f64:Eq (f64 is PartialEq-only, Rust parity).

rules.title: == / != on bounded type variable dispatches to Eq method
rules.statement: == / != where the left operand is a type variable whose bounds (transitively, through supertraits) provide an `eq` method desugar to an auto-ref'd eq/ne method call dispatched after monomorphization; if more than one trait in scope provides `eq`, the call is tagged with trait Eq for disambiguation. Absent an eq-providing bound, falls through to the generic operator check.

rules.title: == / != on same-named enums requires structural Eq impl for payload enums
rules.statement: == / != between two enums of the same name route to the enum's eq/ne impl (a 2-param candidate keyed `EnumName__eq`, concrete or generic) when one exists, auto-borrowing operands; a payload-less (C-like) enum without an impl falls through to discriminant comparison, while a payload-carrying enum with no Eq/PartialEq impl is rejected.

rules.title: Bare enum-literal operand re-lowered with peer's concrete type
rules.statement: In an enum == / != where one operand is a bare enum literal (no type-args, e.g. Option::None) and the other carries concrete type-args, the bare operand is re-lowered with the peer's enum type as the hint so both sides share the same concrete layout for the eq impl.

rules.title: Diverging operand makes binop type !
rules.statement: If either operand has the never type !, the binary expression type-checks against any operator (no numeric/bool requirement) and its result type is !.

rules.title: Error operand yields error type
rules.statement: If either operand has the error type, the binary expression's result type is the error type (error already reported upstream; no cascade).

rules.title: && and || require bool operands, yield bool
rules.statement: Operators && and || require each operand to be bool or the never type !; the result type is bool.

rules.title: Comparison operators yield bool with compatible operands
rules.statement: Comparison operators {==,!=,<,<=,>,>=} require the two operand types to be mutually compatible (in either direction) and produce type bool.

rules.title: Pointer compared only against integer literal 0
rules.statement: A raw pointer may be compared (== / != / relational) with an integer literal, but the literal must be 0; comparing a pointer with any non-zero literal is an error.

rules.title: Comparison literal must fit the peer integer type
rules.statement: In a comparison where one operand is an integer literal and the other a concrete integer type, the literal value must fit in that type's range; otherwise the comparison is rejected (it could never hold).

rules.title: Arithmetic operators require numeric operands
rules.statement: Arithmetic operators {+,-,*,/,%} require both operands to be numeric; the result type is the unified integer type of the operands when both are integers, otherwise unify_numeric, with a TypeVar operand propagated as the result when the other is an integer literal.

rules.title: Division or remainder by literal zero rejected at compile time
rules.statement: / or % whose right operand is an integer literal 0 is a compile-time error; restricted to untyped IntLit RHS so statically-unreachable guarded divides are not rejected.

rules.title: Integer-literal arithmetic is folded; i64 overflow is rejected
rules.statement: When both arithmetic operands are integer literals with recoverable values, +,-,*,/,% are constant-folded to a single integer literal (of untyped IntLit type); if the fold overflows i64 the expression is rejected rather than silently wrapped.
rules.divergence: Rust folds in the inferred type; Logos folds in i64 and errors on i64 overflow, deferring per-type fit to the coercion site.

rules.title: Arithmetic literal operand must fit the peer integer type
rules.statement: In integer arithmetic where one operand is an integer literal and the other a concrete integer type, the literal value must fit in that concrete type's range.

rules.title: Bitwise/shift operands must be integer (or bool for bitwise-only)
rules.statement: Bitwise operators {&,|,^} require integer or bool operands; shift operators {<<,>>} require integer operands only. The result type is the unified integer type of the operands.

rules.title: Negative literal shift count rejected
rules.statement: << or >> whose right operand is a negative integer literal is a compile-time error.

rules.title: Literal shift count >= LHS bit-width rejected
rules.statement: << or >> whose shift count is a literal value >= the bit-width of the left operand's type is a compile-time error (shifting by >= width is undefined); widths: i8/u8=8, i16/u16=16, i24/u24=24, i32/u32=32, i56/u56=56, i64/u64=64, i128/u128=128, usize/isize=64.

rules.title: Unknown binary operator is an error
rules.statement: A binary operator not in the recognized set is rejected as an unknown binary operator.
